items.why: Consent is the stated trigger, though “before the ambushers act” leaves the precise action somewhat vague.
The syntax clearly distinguishes Abishai’s victim, Ishbi-Benob, from David, whom he rescues.
The intended speaker distinction is recoverable, but “gives the message that he says will happen” is awkward and referentially murky.
It requires distinguishing the 2,600 leaders commanding the army from the officials who mustered it.
The reason is explicit, and the competing explanation is directly negated by “even if.”
Hearing the noise motivates Athaliah’s movement, whereas seeing the king occurs only after she arrives.
Zechariah provides the instruction, while Amaziah is mentioned only as Uzziah’s moral example.
The question tests the important difference between the first three-party covenant and the following king-people covenant.
The off-duty companies receive the temple-for-the-king assignment, unlike the three companies going on duty.
Resolving “him” requires distinguishing the skeptical officer from the man of God who issued the warning.
“The news” merely repeats the passage’s label and does not provide the content of what was reported.
Jehoiada gives the weapons, while David is only their former owner.
Jonathan kills one descendant, but the concluding statement credits all four deaths to David and his men collectively.
The king is identified indirectly as the messenger’s master, making the murderer reference a substantive inference.
The ordered accounts of the two Gob battles establish Sibbekai as the first killer.
The letter heading plainly distinguishes Claudius Lysias as sender from Felix as addressee.
The prophecy assigns the future sacrifice of the priests to Josiah, not to Jeroboam standing nearby.
Interpreting the king’s quoted reconstruction shows that capture is to be followed by entry into the city.
The final sentence explicitly assigns presentation of the case to the man’s accusers, not to the earlier-mentioned council.
The warning addresses the man of God from Judah, while the old prophet is the person delivering it.
The men reject both staying and entering the city and instead decide to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The plural pronouns refer to Sceva’s seven sons, who are beaten by the possessed man and flee.
The Arameans regard the Hittite and Egyptian kings as the attackers and Israel’s king only as the one who hired them.
The contrast with the cavalry resolves the returners, though calling them simply “the soldiers” is slightly overbroad.
The command “Seize him” targets the man of God, but the distinction is a fairly direct pronoun resolution.
The negation cleanly contrasts what Jeroboam fails to do with the priestly appointments he does make.
The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the people’s plundering, while reaching the Jordan occurs earlier.
The question distinguishes the new plan to report the discovery from the earlier wrongdoing of hiding valuables.
The two centurions receive the preparation order; the soldiers are personnel to be assembled under that order.
The reply to the officer’s doubt is the personal warning that he will see the food but not eat it, not the preceding price prophecy.
Paul explicitly assigns the message to the young man, despite Paul himself directing the centurion.
A complete answer requires collecting three opponent groups and excluding the Ammonites, who instead bring tribute.
The singular subject Uzziah remains the antecedent of “he,” while the workers are introduced only as his laborers.
Azariah and the other priests follow Uzziah, who had already entered the temple.
Within the old prophet’s claimed command, “him” refers to the man of God who is to be brought back to eat and drink.
The king requests prayer, but the man of God is the one who actually intercedes.
The event sequence clearly places mobilizing the army before marching and laying siege.
Jotham’s succession follows Uzziah’s burial, whereas Isaiah’s recording is mentioned earlier.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet is the one who mounts it.
Following the male pronouns across two prophets is necessary to identify the departing man of God as the lion’s victim.
Paul’s intended departure is explicitly given as the reason, while the lamps have no plausible causal role.
Interpreting the women’s quoted first-person references shows that the speaking woman’s son was eaten first.
Talking until daylight is the last stated action before Paul leaves; eating occurs earlier.
The passage grammatically attributes the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death rather than merely to the people’s rejoicing.
The practitioners burn the assembled scrolls before their value is calculated.
The passage distinguishes the priests hurrying Uzziah out from his own eagerness caused by the divine affliction.
The trampled person is the officer assigned to the gate, not the king who appointed him.
The explicit sword order applies to anyone following the woman, although the woman herself is also subsequently executed.
The quoted arrangement assigns the other woman’s son to tomorrow, though the nested viewpoint makes the wording mildly taxing.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward places it in his tomb.
Only the evil spirits are said to leave, but “on the items’ arrival” is an unnatural description of the event.
Joash is clearly the hidden child, but identifying him indirectly as “Ahaziah’s son” makes the stem unnecessarily cumbersome.
The people take Uzziah for the stated purpose of making him king; Amaziah’s death is background rather than that purpose.
The Sanhedrin is to petition, but the commander is the person expected to bring Paul before the council.
